definition: Curtail means to cut something back or cut it short, so that it goes on — but at a reduced level.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word curtail. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know curtail should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The park curtailed its evening hours after the storm damage, closing the gates at six instead of ten.
Trim is gentler than curtail: trimming shaves a little off the edges, while curtailing cuts a thing back sharply enough that everyone notices what is missing.
Abolish goes further than curtail: a curtailed service still runs, only less of it, while an abolished one is ended outright and wiped from the books.

to hold something back or keep it in check — restraint applied, while the thing may carry on much as before. Curtail actually cuts: after curtailing, there is measurably less of the thing than there was.
to shave small amounts off the edges, often for neatness or thrift. Curtail is the deeper, harder cut, usually imposed from above — hours, budgets, and freedoms get curtailed, and everyone feels it.

Curtail means to cut something back or cut it short, so that it goes on — but at a reduced level.
Mid-drought, the vineyard curtailed irrigation by half: the vines still drank twice a week, but each row got minutes of water where it once had hours.
That is the shape of curtailing: the thing survives, smaller.
The vines are still watered — just less.
If the pumps had been shut off for good, curtail would be the wrong verb; the word always leaves a remainder.
Curtail is the administrator's knife: schedules, budgets, services, rights, and liberties get curtailed — extents, not shapes.
It promises two things at once: a real cut, and a remainder.
Prune the roses and trim the hedge; curtail the watering schedule.
And when nothing survives the decision at all, reach for abolish or scrap — curtail always leaves something running.

curtail: Abolish goes further than curtail: a curtailed service still runs, only less of it, while an abolished one is ended outright and wiped from the books.
The regional rail authority had promised riders a decade of growth.
Instead, last spring it announced it would curtail weekend service, cutting Saturday trains from twenty to nine.
Officials insisted the line was not closing; the trains still ran, only fewer of them.
Riders felt the difference immediately, waiting on platforms that had once cleared every half hour.
Transit advocates said the distinction mattered: a reduced service can be rebuilt, but the shrinking was real, and everyone who rode the line felt what was missing.
